organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Restructured into regional offices after the territorial caliphate collapsed in 2017. Most senior leadership is believed to be in Syria.

organizations.name: Islamic State al-Furqan regional office
organizations.notes: Responsible for Turkey and Europe. Formerly based in Turkey, now largely in Syria. Detailed in UN monitoring team reports.

organizations.name: US Central Command
organizations.notes: Announced the Aleppo helicopter raid and issues monthly statements on raids in Syria.

organizations.name: Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS)
organizations.notes: Former al-Qaeda affiliate that disavowed al-Qaeda. Has cracked down on Hurras al-Din.

organizations.name: Hurras al-Din
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda branch in Syria formed about five years ago from al-Qaeda loyalists who split from HTS. The UN estimates 2,000–2,500 members. Receives direct orders from Saif al-Adel.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Propaganda arm is As-Sahab. Weathered bin Laden's death and the split with the Islamic State well in most theaters, but lost Syria and Iraq.

organizations.name: As-Sahab
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda Central's propaganda arm.

organizations.name: Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan
aliases: movement of the Taliban in Pakistan
organizations.notes: Formed 2007 with al-Qaeda help. At least 8 groups have joined in 2023 and about 30 since 2020. Revived and killing roughly 1,000 Pakistanis. Sheltered by the Afghan Taliban.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: In full control of Afghanistan and expanding its security forces by one third. Shelters the TTP and al-Qaeda.

organizations.name: Government of Pakistan
organizations.notes: The hosts accuse it of sponsoring the Afghan Taliban for 'strategic depth' while its own people are killed by the TTP.

organizations.name: Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP)
organizations.notes: Described as conducting 'pinprick attacks' and a threat to the Taliban.

organizations.name: National Resistance Front (NRF)
organizations.notes: Tajik, Panjshir-based resistance. Last holdout against the Taliban in Panjshir and now shifting to guerrilla tactics.

organizations.name: Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF)
organizations.notes: Primarily former Afghan military commanders, mostly Pashtun.

organizations.name: Afghan Resistance Front
organizations.notes: Mostly former military officers of mixed ethnicities.

organizations.name: Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM)
aliases: Group for Support of Islam and Muslims
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda's main Sahel and West Africa branch. Lost most of rural Menaka to IS Sahel despite fierce resistance, including suicide car bombs.

organizations.name: Islamic State Sahel Province
organizations.notes: Formed in 2015 after a split from al-Qaeda-linked groups. Effectively controls Menaka region outside the town, its largest territorial gain.

organizations.name: Wagner Group
organizations.notes: Present only inside Menaka town and not operating offensively against IS Sahel.

organizations.name: UN peacekeeping force in Mali
organizations.notes: Operates only inside Menaka town.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
rivals: African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS)
organizations.notes: Al-Qaeda's East Africa branch. Alienated central Somalia clans through taxation and forced recruitment but is popular among many southern clans.

organizations.name: Ma'awiisley
organizations.notes: Clan militias backing the government counteroffensive in central Somalia since September 2022.

organizations.name: Somali government
organizations.notes: Claims about 3,000 Shabaab fighters killed since September 2022, which the hosts find implausible.

organizations.name: African Union Transition Mission in Somalia
organizations.notes: Has troops from Kenya, Ethiopia, Djibouti, Uganda and Burundi. About 3,500 peacekeepers have died since 2007.

organizations.name: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Its periodic reports detail IS regional offices and Saif al-Adel's orders to Hurras al-Din.

organizations.name: Jubaland
organizations.notes: Semi-autonomous region under Ahmed Madobe with its own paramilitary forces, already fighting Shabaab in the south.

organizations.name: African Union
organizations.notes: AU peacekeepers are deployed in Somalia. Hosts say some contributing countries are motivated mainly by payment from the EU, with the US paying much of the EU payroll. The hosts cite roughly 3,500 AU peacekeeper deaths since 2007, mostly Ugandan and Burundian. They say countries may be looking to disengage and that withdrawal dates may be pushed back again.

organizations.name: European Union
organizations.notes: Pays AU troop contributors in Somalia. Hosts say the US pays a large share of the EU payroll.

organizations.name: United States government
organizations.notes: Provides minimal resources in Somalia, per the hosts, and funds much of the EU payroll for AU troops.

organizations.name: Voice of America
organizations.notes: Cited for a report on AU peacekeeper deaths in Somalia.

organizations.name: Uganda
organizations.notes: Contributes the majority of AU peacekeeper dead, together with Burundi, and is named as a Shabaab target.

organizations.name: Burundi
organizations.notes: Contributes the majority of AU peacekeeper dead, together with Uganda.

places.name: Kenya

places.significance: Named as a country threatened by Shabaab. Its troops make up much of the AU peacekeeper dead.

events.description: CENTCOM announced a helicopter raid in Aleppo targeting senior Islamic State official Abdul Hadi Muhammad Haji Ali, accused of plotting attacks in Europe and the region.
The previous week CENTCOM announced action against a Yemeni IS official in eastern Syria.
The US designated al-Qaeda ideologue and Hurras al-Din commander Sami al-Raddi.
Collapse of the Islamic State's territorial caliphate, after which IS restructured around regional offices.
At least eight groups joined the TTP so far in 2023, roughly 30 since 2020.
Fall of the Afghan government to the Taliban, which Roggio had predicted would happen by the end of summer.
US congressional hearing on the Afghanistan withdrawal, with a witness who had predicted the Afghan military would hold.
IS Sahel began an offensive in Menaka and routed JNIM and allied Tuareg and Dawsahak militias from most rural areas.
Islamic State Sahel Province formed after a split from other al-Qaeda branches in West Africa.
The Somali government and Ma'awiisley clan militias started a counteroffensive against al-Shabaab in central Somalia.
President Hassan Sheikh announced the end of phase one and the start of phase two of the counteroffensive in southern Somalia, involving federal troops.
Kenya, Ethiopia and Djibouti announced additional troops to Somalia outside African Union command, as part of a joint force.
Al-Shabaab overran a small Somali military base and published photos of dozens of dead troops, while the Somali government denied it.
Somali politicians announced 'phase two' of the offensive against Shabaab and declared victory. The hosts say this may not age well.
Start of the period over which the hosts cite roughly 3,500 AU peacekeeper deaths in Somalia, mostly Ugandan and Burundian, per a Voice of America report.
The hosts recall a Shabaab bomb detonated on a plane, thought to be part of a wider plot. They say it led to airport rules requiring laptops to be turned on at screening.

key_claims: The US raid in Aleppo, far from US positions in northeast Syria, shows how dangerous the hosts think the new generation of IS plotters is, and counters claims that IS is defeated.
Most senior IS leaders are in Syria; US operations in Iraq are not capturing high-level IS officials.
Hurras al-Din is still operationally important to al-Qaeda: the UN says Saif al-Adel, likely the new emir, directly orders it, possibly from Iran.
The TTP is reviving, absorbing about 30 small groups since 2020, and the Pakistani state tolerates this to preserve its ties with the Afghan Taliban.

The Afghan Taliban shelter the TTP and al-Qaeda, while the scattered anti-Taliban resistance groups (NRF, Afghanistan Freedom Front, Afghan Resistance Front) must unite and need foreign funding to matter.
IS Sahel has effectively taken control of Mali's Menaka region from JNIM, its first major territorial gain, leaving only al-Qaeda able to challenge it.
Shabaab is still attacking Somali positions, including in central Somalia, despite the government's claims of progress and 'phase two'.
Some African contributing countries stay in Somalia mainly because the EU, largely funded by the US, pays them.
Several AU troop-contributing countries may be looking to disengage, and AU withdrawal dates may be pushed back again.
Resources committed against Shabaab by the US and African countries are minimal, so defeating the group is unlikely given the history of repeated interventions.
Roughly 3,500 AU peacekeepers have died in Somalia since 2007, mostly Ugandan and Burundian.
Shabaab is a global threat, as shown by its aviation plots, flight-training arrests and a plane bombing the hosts link to 2016 airport laptop screening.
